To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the thermal evolution of the π–σ spectral functions is dominated by the thermal evolution of their maximum and that the latter is governed by the thermal evolution of the σ mass.
at T =0 the σ meson is a narrow resonance, and that it becomes increasingly broadened and less prominent as temperature is raised.
the spectral function at T∼1 m π has a pronounced peak and a width of the order of 0.5 GeV, and that the peak is shifted to lower values of the energy by 100 MeV.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the spectral functions of the π and the σ meson are in a very good agreement with the experimental data for temperatures up to T∼1 GeV.

the σ meson is not a good candidate for the observed resonance at ∼1 GeV in the vector current correlator at finite temperature, but it could well correspond to the broad resonance in the scalar current correlator at ∼1.2 GeV.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that the spectral function of the σ mesons is a rather complicated function of temperature, and that the spectral function is not a good measure of the mass of the σ mesonic state.
the spectral function is a good measure for the meson mass at low and medium temperatures, but that it loses its meaning at high temperatures.
the thermal evolution of the σ mesons is qualitatively similar to that of pions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in contrast to the case at zero temperature, the spectral function of the π–σ composite system is not dominated by a narrow resonance at finite temperature.
the spectral function of the σ mesons at high temperatures is dominated by the two-particle states, which are the only states with a nonvanishing spectral weight.
the thermal evolution of the σ mesons spectral function can be described in terms of the spectral functions of the elementary fields.
